claims.text: The target material is a multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy containing at least two phases.
The phases are electrochemically distinct, with a nobler FCC or ordered phase and a more active BCC/B2 phase.
The multiphase alloy forms a thin protective oxide film at elevated temperature.
Breakdown of a transient protective oxide drives accelerated degradation during simultaneous wear and corrosion.
Mechanical wear preferentially removes or damages the protective oxide at phase boundaries.
Oxide disruption exposes the heterogeneous microstructure and establishes micro-galvanic cells at phase boundaries.
In the proposed micro-galvanic cells, the nobler phase is cathodic and the less stable phase is anodic.
Micro-galvanic coupling accelerates localized dissolution of the anodic phase.
Localized anodic dissolution weakens the surface mechanically and thereby increases subsequent wear.
Corrosion-assisted weakening and wear-assisted oxide removal form a positive feedback loop.
Elevated-temperature wear and corrosion are relevant in approximately the 500–900 °C range and in oxidizing or molten-salt environments.
The mechanism applies when the wear load disrupts surface oxides but does not cause immediate gross mechanical failure.
A homogeneous single-phase HEA baseline forms a more uniform and stable oxide layer than the multiphase eutectic alloy.
The multiphase eutectic alloy will exhibit greater total material loss than a matched homogeneous single-phase HEA under identical coupled conditions.
The multiphase eutectic alloy will exhibit greater wear depth than the single-phase baseline.
The multiphase eutectic alloy will exhibit higher corrosion current density than the single-phase baseline.
Corrosion damage will be localized preferentially at phase boundaries.
The increase in degradation may be on the order of two- to three-fold, although this scaling is explicitly uncertain.
The balance between oxide repair and oxide removal during cyclic wear is temperature- and rate-dependent.
